blocks.text: 1. Recursive Chunking

blocks.alt: A document tries separators in order to produce more natural chunks

blocks.text: Recursive Chunking covers a smarter way to split text by trying multiple boundary types, building directly on fixed chunking's simplicity.
It falls back through an ordered list of separators until chunks fit the target size.
2. Fixed Chunking's Blind Spot
As covered under ignoring content boundaries in Fixed Chunking, a fixed cutoff cuts wherever the count runs out, with no regard for structure.
Recursive chunking was designed specifically to address that blind spot.
3. An Ordered List Of Separators

blocks.alt: A paragraph break, sentence break, and word break form an ordered list

blocks.text: Paragraph breaks, then sentence breaks, then word breaks form an ordered list of preferred cut points.
The algorithm tries the most natural boundary first, before falling back to a cruder one.

blocks.text: 4. The Recursive Splitting Process

blocks.alt: A chunk too large gets split again with the next separator

blocks.text: It splits on the first separator, then recurses into any piece still too large.
This repeats with the next separator down the list until every piece fits.
5. Falling Back Gracefully

blocks.alt: A failing preferred separator falls back to the next separator

blocks.text: If no paragraph or sentence break exists within a piece, the algorithm falls back to a word or character break.
This guarantees every chunk still respects the target size, even as a last resort.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A long, unbroken block of text with no punctuation still produces correctly sized chunks under recursive chunking, since the algorithm falls all the way back to a word or character split when nothing else is available.

blocks.text: 6. Preserving More Natural Structure

blocks.alt: Fixed chunking is compared against recursive chunking, which respects structure

blocks.text: Most cuts land at a paragraph or sentence boundary rather than mid sentence.
Recursive chunking directly reduces the broken meaning at boundaries problem covered in Fixed Chunking.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Comparing the same document under both strategies typically shows recursive chunking producing noticeably more chunks that begin and end on complete sentences, directly improving how coherent each individual chunk reads on its own.

blocks.text: 7. Still Not Fully Semantic

blocks.alt: Recursive chunking is compared against semantic chunking, which is meaning-based

blocks.text: Recursive chunking respects structural boundaries, but still ignores meaning itself.
As covered under many ways to split in Why Chunking, semantic chunking, covered later in this module, goes a step further.

blocks.text: 8. Recursive Chunking As A Default Choice
Balancing simplicity against structural awareness makes recursive chunking a common default.
It is widely used across real world RAG pipelines as a solid, general purpose starting point.
9. Recognizing When Recursive Chunking Is The Right Choice

blocks.alt: Needing a general-purpose default points toward recursive chunking

blocks.text: General purpose text with paragraphs and sentences suits recursive chunking well.
Content where meaning matters more than structure, by contrast, needs semantic chunking, covered later in this module.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using only a single separator instead of an ordered list of fallback options.
Forgetting to recurse into pieces that are still too large after the first split.
Assuming recursive chunking understands meaning when it only respects structural boundaries.
Choosing a separator order that does not match the actual structure of the source documents.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Recursive chunking falls back through an ordered list of separators until chunks fit the target size.
It was designed specifically to address fixed chunking's blind spot for content structure.
The typical separator order tries paragraph breaks, then sentence breaks, then word breaks.
It splits on the first separator, then recurses into any piece still too large.
A graceful fallback guarantees every chunk still respects the target size as a last resort.
Most cuts land at natural boundaries, reducing the broken meaning problem from fixed chunking.
It still respects only structure, not the actual meaning of the text, unlike semantic chunking.
It is a common, general purpose default across many real world RAG pipelines.
Next up: Semantic Chunking, covering how meaning itself can guide where chunks are split.
